readerTitle: Why the $40,000 promise lost to the $2,800 one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (건물 설비 유지보수 업체, 식품 도매 유통) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 비즈니스 케이스는 판매자를 위한 자료가 아니라, 구매자가 회의실에 없던 결재자에게 다시 설명할 때 쓰는 도구다. 그래서 숫자가 크기보다 구매자가 직접 확인할 수 있어야 이긴다.
misconception: 절감액이나 ROI 숫자가 클수록 설득력이 높다. 업계 평균 수치를 보여주면 충분하다.

sources.text: 컨설팅형 영업의 일반적 실무 개념 (현상 유지 비용, 변경 비용, 손익분기 가정)

factChecks.note: $40,000 경쟁 제안은 출처 없는 '업계 평균'으로 설정한 가상 수치입니다. 실제 업계 통계를 암시하지 않도록 카드 문장에서 'industry averages'라고만 표현했습니다.
도매 사례는 수치를 지정하지 않은 가상 상황입니다. 실제 연구나 통계를 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the $40,000 promise lost to the $2,800 one
body: Two maintenance firms bid to service the heating and cooling in a mid-sized office building.
The first promised the building manager **$40,000 a year** in savings. The second promised $2,800. The second firm won the contract.

image.label: Two proposals on a desk, one with a huge number, one with a small one
image.brief: 사무실 책상 위 제안서 두 장. 왼쪽은 커다란 "$40,000"이 화려하게 적혀 있고, 오른쪽은 작은 "$2,800"과 손글씨 메모, 청구서 사본이 클립으로 붙어 있음. 오른쪽 제안서에 도장이 찍혀 있음. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which proposal would you send?
body: You run a building maintenance firm. You're offering a preventive service contract for $600 a month. The building manager likes you, but the owner signs anything over $5,000.
Which proposal gives you the best chance?

options.text: Show savings based on industry averages: up to $40,000 a year
options.feedback: The big number grabs attention. But the owner can't check it, and the manager can't defend it.

options.text: Ask for last year's repair invoices and build a modest estimate from them
options.feedback: You get a smaller number, but one the owner can verify. It costs you time and a bit of trust-building to get the invoices.

options.text: Skip the numbers and stress your quality and response times
options.feedback: Quality matters, and it's easy to say. But it gives the manager nothing to bring to the owner when the price comes up.

cards.title: The big number fell apart in one question.
body: The manager took the $40,000 proposal to the owner. The owner asked one question: *where does this number come from?*
The manager didn't know. Neither did the proposal. It came from averages across buildings the owner had never seen.
The second firm had asked for the building's own repair invoices. The owner recognized every line. The decision took ten minutes.

cards.title: The case that won, line by line.
body: The firm said, "Our other clients usually do better than half, but let's plan on half." Even if repairs fall only 36%, the contract pays for itself.

cards.title: The business case
body: A **business case** is a short argument, in the buyer's own numbers, that changing is worth more than it costs.
It has three parts: what the current situation costs, what the change costs, and the gap between them, with the assumptions shown.
The comparison is not you versus a rival. It's you versus doing nothing, which is what most buyers choose.

image.label: A scale weighing the cost of doing nothing against the cost of change
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Cost of doing nothing"(청구서 더미), 오른쪽 접시에 "Cost of change"(계약서 한 장). 왼쪽이 약간 더 무거움. 아래에 작은 글씨로 "Assumption: 50% fewer repairs".

cards.title: You're writing for someone who wasn't in the room.
body: Your contact rarely signs alone. They carry your proposal to a boss, an owner or a finance person who never met you.
That person trusts numbers they already know, like their own invoices, hours and losses. A cautious assumption they can see beats a bold one they can't check.
So a business case is really a tool you hand your buyer to make the sale for you.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the same rule applies: "save 10 hours a week per user" lands better when it comes from the customer's own time logs, multiplied by their own seat count, than from a benchmark on your website.

cards.title: A case can be built badly, too.
body: Some buyers won't share their numbers. Then build a range together and let them fill in the blanks, rather than guessing for them.
Don't fake precision. Things like safety or reputation can matter a lot without a dollar figure. Name them separately instead of inventing one.
And size the effort to the deal. A $300 sale doesn't need a spreadsheet.

cards.title: Now you're a food wholesaler.
body: You supply produce to a family grocery with three stores. You want them to switch to smaller, more frequent deliveries, which cost a little more per order. The owner says they're happy with weekly deliveries.
What's your next move?

options.text: Tell them clients like them cut spoilage by up to a third
options.feedback: It sounds strong, but it's your number, not theirs. The owner has no reason to believe it applies to their stores.

options.text: Ask what they threw away last month, then estimate savings with a cautious assumption
options.feedback: It takes an extra conversation, but you get a case built from their own losses that they can check against their records.

options.text: Offer a 10% discount on the first three months
options.feedback: It lowers the risk of trying. But it gives away margin and still doesn't show why the switch is worth it after month three.

cards.title: Build the case from their numbers, not yours.
body: A smaller number the buyer can check beats a bigger one they have to take on faith. Show the cost of doing nothing, the cost of change, and your assumption.
**Try it today:** for one open deal, write down one number you'd need from the customer's own records to prove your value. Then ask for it.
